q: A plain roast chicken is famously the most accommodating dish on any menu. What makes it so?
opts: It is moderate in weight, fat and flavour
It has almost no flavour of its own to speak of
It is unusually high in acid
It carries a great deal of salt in the skin
exp: Nothing about it is extreme, so it sits comfortably beside a white or a red and rarely embarrasses either. It is the dish to reach for when a table cannot agree, and the reason so many producers name it when asked what to drink with their own wine.

q: Roast leg of lamb, studded with garlic and rosemary, is carved at the table. Which of these bottles is the enduring answer?
opts: A red Bordeaux
A dry Marsala
An oaked white Rioja
A Mosel Kabinett
exp: The fat and protein in the lamb soften Cabernet and Merlot tannin, and the cedary, herbal edge of a claret runs alongside the rosemary rather than across it. The pairing is old enough that Cabernet-based reds appear beside lamb on menus in countries that grow neither.

q: The old rule pairs white with fish and red with meat. Which dish shows it up most clearly?
opts: Grilled tuna, seared rare
Poached turbot in a light stock
Steamed sea bass with lemon
Raw scallops dressed with lime
exp: Tuna is dense, meaty and best served pink, and a light red handles it better than most whites do. The other three are exactly the dishes the old rule was written for, and it serves them perfectly well, which is why it survives as a starting point rather than as a law.

q: The same regional wine keeps turning up beside the same regional dish, century after century. What is the soundest explanation?
opts: The dish is always cooked with that wine
Regional law requires the combination
The two grew up together
The wine is cheaper in its own region than anywhere else
exp: Cooks and growers in the same place spent centuries correcting one another, and what survived is a pairing that works rather than a rule anyone sat down and wrote. It is why what grows together goes together is a better first guess than any chart, and why a regional menu is the easiest place to start.

q: A holiday table carries a mild roast bird surrounded by sweet, salty and sharp accompaniments. Which pour is the most forgiving?
opts: The most tannic red on the list
A very sweet dessert wine
A bone-dry, austere white
A fruity, low-tannin red or a full rose
exp: The bird is mild but the table is crowded, so the wine has to be forgiving rather than impressive, and low tannin with generous fruit collides with the fewest things on the plate. Cranberry sauce on its own is enough to strip a dry tannic red of everything it had.

q: Nothing about the bottle has changed, yet the sip taken after the starter tastes oddly and distinctly sweet. Which vegetable did the guest just eat?
opts: Globe artichoke
Cucumber
Fennel
Roasted red pepper
exp: The effect is strong enough that this vegetable has a reputation as unpairable, and it is why a kitchen cooking for a wine dinner tends to keep it off the menu altogether. Plenty of lemon and olive oil, or roasting it hard, softens the problem without removing it.

q: Which starter coats the palate so thoroughly that everything poured after it is muffled?
opts: A clear beef consomme
A soft-boiled egg with buttered soldiers
Grilled prawns with garlic, chilli and parsley
A tomato and basil salad dressed with oil
exp: A rich yolk leaves a film that blunts whatever follows, which is why egg dishes have an awkward reputation with wine and why brunch menus reach for something sharp and sparkling. Acidity and bubbles are the counter, and both of them work by clearing rather than by matching.

q: A first-course salad is being dressed for a menu built around wine. Which change gives the wine the best chance?
opts: Use less vinegar, and more oil and lemon
Add sugar to the dressing
Use a stronger vinegar so it stands out
Chill the salad harder
exp: Sharp vinegar flattens whatever is drunk after it, and no bottle on the list repairs a dressing that aggressive, so the fix belongs in the kitchen rather than the cellar. Citrus is gentler and oil buffers the acid, which is the cheapest adjustment available to anyone.

q: A very dark, bitter chocolate torte closes the meal. Which pour is the least suitable?
opts: A sweet red made from dried grapes
A sweet red fortified wine
A rich, raisiny sweet Sherry
A dry, tannic red
exp: Two failures arrive at once: the bitterness of the chocolate and the bitterness of the tannin pile up, and there is no sugar in a dry wine to meet the sugar in the pudding. Everything else here is sweet enough and soft enough to stand beside it.

q: A double espresso is drunk before the dessert wine is poured. What has that done to the wine?
opts: Made the wine seem more tannic
Left a bitterness behind that flattens it
Cleared the palate for the wine that follows
Nothing at all
exp: Strong coffee is bitter, hot and lingering, and all three get in the way of whatever is tasted next. The order is the fix rather than the wine: pour the sweet glass first and let the coffee close the meal.

q: A tinny, almost metallic taste comes up the moment a tannic red meets the fish course. Which fish was on the plate?
opts: Steamed cod
Grilled mackerel
Grilled sole
Poached turbot
exp: The oil in a fish of this kind reacting with the wine is the usual explanation, and the taste is unmistakable once it has been met. Lean white fish does not produce it at all, which shows the fault belongs to the oil rather than to fish in general.

q: Fresh pineapple and lime finish the meal, and the sweet wine beside them tastes thick and flat. What is the difficulty?
opts: The fruit is far sweeter than the wine is
The fruit is sharper than the wine
The fruit carries a tannin of its own
The fruit is being served too warm to taste
exp: A sweet wine needs acidity of its own to stand beside sharp fruit, or it reads heavy and dull the moment the two meet. It is the same reason the great dessert wines are prized for their acid quite as much as for their sugar.

q: Guests arrive and want a glass before the menus have even been opened. Which style makes the best aperitif?
opts: Dry, light and high in acid
Tannic and high in alcohol
Heavily oaked and warming
Sweet, rich and full-bodied
exp: A first glass is there to sharpen the appetite rather than satisfy it, so anything sweet or heavy dulls the palate before the food has arrived. Dry sparkling wine, dry Sherry and a crisp unoaked white are all built for exactly this job.

q: Cheese comes before the pudding in France and after it in Britain. What does the French order make easier?
opts: The sweet wine has to be opened first
No wine is served with cheese in either order
The cheese course still needs its own red either way
The red from the main course can carry on
exp: Putting the cheese first lets one bottle serve two courses and keeps the sweet wine for the sweet course, where relative sweetness decides everything. It is a practical arrangement as much as a national habit, and it is worth knowing which order a kitchen follows before writing the pairings.

q: Thin, hot consomme opens the meal. What is the standard advice about wine with soup?
opts: Pour little or nothing
Pour the sweetest wine of the meal
Pour the same wine as the main course
Pour the biggest red of the meal
exp: Two liquids at once give the palate no contrast of texture, and a hot bowl blunts aroma besides. The traditional exception is a fortified wine such as a dry Sherry or a Sercial Madeira, which has the concentration to be noticed at all.

q: A sorbet lands between the fish course and the meat course. What is it doing, in wine terms?
opts: Adding sweetness to the next wine
Clearing the palate between two very different wines
Signalling the end of the white wines
Replacing the need for a wine with the meat course
exp: The point is that the wine following it is met fresh rather than through the last of the fish, which matters most when the two pours have nothing in common. Its own cold and sugar are the reason nothing worth tasting is poured alongside it.
